data.title: Releasing kadence
body: # Releasing kadence
A release is `npm publish`. It is the one thing this project does that cannot
be undone: the unpublish window is 72 hours and discouraged, after which the
only remedies are `npm deprecate` and a patch. There is no feature flag to
turn off, no percentage to roll back to, and no dashboard that will tell you
something went wrong.
That last one is a decision, not an omission. kadence makes no network request
and sends no telemetry, so **nothing is observable after publication**. Every
check below is front-loaded for that reason: what is not caught here is caught
by a person in a repository we will never see.
And the blast radius is not an outage. A bad release writes events into
somebody's git history, where an append-only journal means they cannot be
removed — only added to.
## 1. What CI proves
Green on `main` for every Node in the matrix. If any of these is red the
release stops; none of them is a judgement call.
- [ ] `npm test` — the full suite, on every Node version in `engines`
- [ ] `npm run typecheck` — clean
- [ ] `npm run build` — from a clean `dist/`, not a leftover one
- [ ] `npm audit --omit=dev` — no vulnerability at any level
- [ ] The lazily-imported TUI never entered the fast path (CI greps `dist/cli.js`)
## 2. What CI cannot prove
Everything in this section has shipped past a green suite in this project
before. That is why the section exists, and why each line names its incident.
- [ ] **Run the TUI by hand.** `node dist/cli.js ui` and use it. Four bugs
reached a release this way: keys routed to two handlers, a key stream
that stopped, Ctrl-D deleting a task, an invisible selection. All at the
boundary with the terminal, all invisible to the suite.
- [ ] **Check one thing at real size, through a pipe.** Every `--json`
response over 128 KiB came back truncated when stdout was a pipe — which
is how agents read it — because `process.exit()` does not wait for an
async write. 418 tests passed over it because every fixture was small.
- [ ] **Measure, do not assume.** `prime`, `ready`, `task list`, `search`
against the 200 ms budget, on a journal the size of a real one. A
guardrail that measures the layer below the command is how a warm read
of the whole journal survived every perf test (KAD-45).
- [ ] **Drive the build in this working tree.** `node dist/cli.js`, never
`kadence` on PATH. The global install was 0.1.5 while the repository was
at 0.4.1, and `prime` did not exist in it.
## 3. What leaves the building
Run this whenever the journal gained events in bulk — a migration, an import,
anything not typed by hand. It is not a formality: the documentation migration
put three documents naming people into a public repository's journal, and only
an audit before the push caught them.
- [ ] **`npm pack --dry-run`** — read the file list. `.kadence/` must not be
in it; the journal belongs to the repository, not to the package.
- [ ] **No person is the subject of anything new in `.kadence/`.** ADR-007
names which files that rules out, and `strategy.md` states the rule:
never put a person in the journal — it is append-only, so somebody who
asks to be removed could never be erased. Read that decision; do not
pattern-match for it. A scan for handles and tables finds the file that
warns about itself and misses the three that hide a person in prose.
- [ ] **No credential shapes, no machine paths** in anything newly committed.
- [ ] **The author on every new commit is the address the project publishes
under**, not a work one.
## 4. Version and contract
- [ ] **Version chosen against what actually changed**, not against effort.
Pre-1.0, anything that changes a default or removes a field is a minor
bump, not a patch.
- [ ] **`kadence schema --json` still holds.** Within `kadence/v1` a field may
be added, never renamed or removed. A *default* may change — 0.7.0
changed three — but then the changelog says so in a table with the flag
that restores the old answer.
- [ ] **`CHANGELOG.md`** — what changed, and for anything breaking, an
Upgrading section a reader can act on without reading the diff.
- [ ] **The reasoning is in the journal, not only in the commit.**
`kadence decision list` should explain every choice this release made.
## 5. The two things that are only in someone's head
Both were nearly forgotten in 0.7.0. That is what this document is for.
- [ ] **`npm run reference` — and do it *after* publishing, not before.**
`prepublishOnly` runs the build, and the build wipes `dist/`, so a
`reference.json` generated beforehand is gone by the time the tarball is
made. Then copy it into the site repository and commit it there: the site
takes the command reference as a committed file rather than a build-time
download, so a new command does not reach the docs until somebody moves
the file.
Its absence from the tarball is correct and not a mistake — DEC-4: the
package ships the generator, `scripts/reference.mjs`, and not the
generated file. A `npm pack --dry-run` that shows `reference.json` is
showing a stale `dist/`, not what will publish.
- [ ] **`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.kadence/README.md` regenerated.** A new
command that is not in the section an agent reads is a command no agent
will use. `kadence init` refreshes the first two and leaves the third
alone — that one is written at first init and has to be regenerated on
purpose.
## 6. Publishing
- [ ] Working tree clean, on `main`, CI green on the merge commit
- [ ] `npm publish` — `prepublishOnly` runs typecheck, tests and build again
- [ ] Tag the release and push the tag
- [ ] `npm view kadence version` agrees with `package.json`
- [ ] **Install it the way a stranger would** — `npm i -g kadence` in a
throwaway directory, `kadence init`, `kadence prime`, `kadence search`.
Not the working tree. The package, from the registry.
## 7. When it is wrong
There is no rollback. There is what is left:
| How long ago | What is possible |
| under 72 hours, nobody depends on it | `npm unpublish kadence@x.y.z` — discouraged, and it breaks anyone who already installed |
| any time | `npm deprecate kadence@x.y.z "…"` and publish a patch. The bad version stays installable |
| an event shape went out wrong | worse than either: it is in users' git history, and the journal is append-only. A fix can only add |
Which is why the last line of section 2 matters more than anything in
section 6: a version that should not have shipped is cheap to catch and
expensive to have shipped.
## One thing publishing itself changes
Adding a document to the journal moves `test/search-relevance.test.ts`.
Publishing this checklist as a document cost one question — a page of release
vocabulary shifts the rarity of a dozen words, and a query that had nothing to
do with releases lost its slot. That is drift, not regression. One question is
normal; the floor sits two below the current rate so that a build breaks on a
ranking change and not on a new document.
- [ ] After adding anything sizeable to the journal, read the recall number the
test prints. It is information whether it passes or not.
## Known, and not a blocker
`npm audit signatures` fails on `blessed@0.1.81`, whose registry signature
carries a public key that expired 2025-01-29; the command aborts on the first
bad signature, so anyone verifying kadence the standard way sees an error that
is not about kadence. Tracked as KAD-47. `npm audit` itself is clean.
